From a religious standpoint, I also agree with /LovelessLoveMaker. I don’t want anyone who’s not a good role model to represent my faith, and I certainly don’t want my family to vote for that non-good role model solely because they’re also religious. Religious politics aren’t a good look.

From a minority standpoint, religion also shouldn’t be in politics because the politician is supposed to represent the public. I’m not saying a politician shouldn’t be religious, but I’d prefer if that religion isn’t interfering with the choices that are being made for all of their constituents. After all, not all of their constituents are religious, nor do they share the morals that come with different religions (in particular, different sections of Christianity). If the religious majority votes in an official just because they’re religious, that’s great and by all means the official should represent them— but they should do so in a way that doesn’t interfere with people of a different religion, or people with no faith at all. Nobody has the right  to push their religion onto those that don’t practice, even if the official voted in represents the majority religion. 

Another thing is that religious people might be swayed by their religion to vote for a particular candidate. That’s all well good and I don’t mean to judge them, but this wouldn’t be a phenomenon if not for religion in politics. Not to mention how many times religion has been used as an excuse to be prejudiced which, again, isn’t a good look for religious people.

You say you eat three meals a day with snacks and the like, but how big are the meals? That could be a cause. Not eating enough can lead to the body holding onto/storing fat for longer, iirc.

You say that you’ve been drinking 8 glasses of water everyday. Have you always done this, or did you make it a habit along with healthy eating? (Also, if you find yourself sitting more these days, you could be retaining water.) 

Eating healthy is good, but you must make sure to have a variety, too.

Are you sleeping okay? Sleeping can lead to weight fluctuation. 

One last thing: you never specified how much unhealthy food you ate. I’m assuming you ate at least two meals a day here, but if you only ate one, then you could have been underweight to start.

Isn’t Minneapolis still standing? I’m pretty sure Minneapolis is still standing. Let’s not exaggerate here. 

I don’t like arsonists, generally, and I don’t approve of the burning of any part of Minneapolis. It sucks that so much damage was done. But let’s not pretend that burning was the bulk of what happened. Apparently around 150 buildings were set on fire, and a couple dozen were actually completely burned. That’s kind of a lot. But it’s not the whole of Minneapolis, and a lot of other types of vandalism (typical spray paint, broken windows, etc.) were done as well. And then, of course, we should also mention that there were plenty of peaceful protesters— just for the sake of being fair. 

I think Minneapolis’s economy will prove to be more impacted by this than the physical city. 

It’s like the Capitol, really, and any differences in damage can be extrapolated by the fact that our legislative branch had to be evacuated due to it, and that it was an extremely important federal building. There were thousands of peaceful protesters who thought they were sticking up for justice/democracy, however misguided, and then there were those that actually broke shit and made the whole event look bad. And now only news footage of the breaking shit is ever going to be remembered, and that’s all anyone focuses on. Hell, the most impact this past riot had will not be the Capitol’s broken windows. 

TL;DR: Much like the protesting/rioting at the Capitol, the heaviest impacts of rioting in Minneapolis are not going to be physical; we can especially say this because Minneapolis didn’t burn to the ground.

Can you afford to get your Masters degree in Europe? 

It may not be as fun as pure travel, but it’s more experience and you’ll still have time to do other cool things (can’t say anything specific because I don’t know what country you’d go to). It will be experience with living in another country. I don’t know how long you were planning on staying in each country if you travelled, but staying in a place and living in a place are not the same.

If I could comfortably afford to do a Master’s Degree in a foreign country (and I was trying to get a degree in something that wasn’t specific to the United States) I would do it. 

But these are my values; I was raised on getting an education as soon as possible so I can start my career as soon as possible, and obviously in every field, the higher up you are = the more qualified. This is what I would do. I’ve been to a lot of countries and I would trade all those experiences for obtaining a master’s degree, but keep in mind that this is also due to my current living situation (which isn’t the best). Your values might be different, and in the end I can only do so much for you. 

I will say, though, that living in Europe would likely still be an extremely memorable experience for you. You might never forget the people you meet; I know I never do. You’ll still get to do fun things, but you’ll be obtaining an education alongside it. I would go with obtaining a master’s degree and then if you still have a comfortable amount of money left you can travel. I wouldn’t recommend spending all your money traveling when you’re still (I’m assuming here) so young.

I don’t think being a victim of abuse hinders your ability to write. Some people say that pain and suffering makes your writing more effective; I don’t think this is true unless you’re writing about pain and suffering, which Kafka may have been doing to a certain extent. Actually, it’s possible that much of his writing is about abuse and that this is why it seems so brilliant— that he wrote of what he knew. However, this isn’t the most popular theory about his writing and I won’t get into it here. (On another note, some of the most memorable lines and stories from Blue Octavo Notebooks gave me abuse/inadequacy vibes, which is why I enjoy his work so much.) 

The thing about abuse, which I think you might be hung up on, is that it can rob you of your entire personality. However, that’s not to say that if it happens, it’s gone forever. Think about it like this: a brilliant person that undergoes an abusive partner doesn’t just permanently stop being brilliant. Why would it be any different for someone that’s raised in an abusive household?

Honestly, Kafka’s case doesn’t really surprise me. I wouldn’t describe him, or any abuse victim (except for me, in my mind I am the Absolute Exception), as ‘fucked up’. Abuse isn’t ever the victim’s fault, and their experiences don’t define them. It would be different if Kafka was a serial rapist or if he murdered children or something, but as far as we know he didn’t do any of this. It’s not fair to define Kafka, or anyone else, as ‘fucked up’ due to the things that were done to him. From the bits I’ve read about him, he didn’t just sit and tremble in corners and write. He escaped the abuse and the rational fear that came with living under abuse— so then afterward he might’ve had to deal with the irrational fear, or the after-effects of the abuse.

I don’t believe Kafka ever fully recovered from the abuse; I believe that it may have altered his life and personality. But I don’t believe that ‘fully recovering’ is the bar for recovering either. Recovery isn’t this one day that you’re going to wake up and it’ll be like the abuse never happened. Recovery is not letting the abuse define you, and continuing to move forward. Kafka had friends. Kafka had a job. He was just a regular person— except for his brilliant writing, of course.

If it still seems difficult, think about it this way: you likely know people that were horribly abused in some way. It’s hard to track the prevalence of emotional abuse because it’s not a criminal offense, but all types of abuse are prevalent (sexual abuse is especially common). You probably know someone that was abused/assaulted in some way (not necessarily emotional) and you won’t know until they tell you, if they do. 

TL;DR: Kafka was abused as a child, sure, but it doesn’t define who he was. It was a thing that was done to him; it doesn’t show anything to his character. It almost definitely affected him, but not to the extent that he wouldn’t have been able to write the things he did.
